Upper bounds — holds for every total

  • \(\widetilde{\deg}(f) = \Omega\big(\sqrt{\mathrm{RC}(f)}\big),\ \text{ i.e. } \mathrm{RC}(f) = O\big(\widetilde{\deg}(f)^2\big)\)
    KulkarniTal16
    Solves a question of Aaronson. Since $\mathrm{QC}(f)=\Theta(\sqrt{\mathrm{RC}(f)})$ [Aaronson08], this says $\widetilde{\deg}(f)=\Omega(\mathrm{QC}(f))$: approximate degree is always at least as good a quantum lower bound as quantum certificate complexity.
  • \(\mathrm{fbs}(f) = O\big(\widetilde{\deg}(f)^2\big)\)
    KulkarniTal16
    Same statement, since $\mathrm{fbs}=\Theta(\mathrm{RC})$.

  • \(\widetilde{\deg}(\mathrm{PARITY}_n) = \mathrm{R}(\mathrm{PARITY}_n) = n\)
    witness: \(\oplus_n\) NS94 BBCMdW01
    Both sides are exactly $n$: parity needs all $n$ queries even at error $1/3$, and no polynomial of degree $<n$ approximates it. Theorem 15 of [BdW02] loses nothing here.

The bound itself, $\widetilde{\deg}\le\mathrm{R}$, is recorded one setting up -- the polynomial method never uses totality -- and inherited here; this record keeps the total-function witness, which makes it tight. The same proof gives $\widetilde{\deg}_\varepsilon(f)\le\mathrm{R}_\varepsilon(f)$ for every error $\varepsilon$, and $\deg(f)\le \mathrm{D}(f)$ in the exact case. The reverse direction is where everything is hard: see \(\mathrm{R}_{\varepsilon}(f)\) vs \(\widetilde{\deg}_{\varepsilon}(f)\) (quartic separation, [ABBLSS17]).

Upper bounds — holds for every partial

  • \(\widetilde{\deg}(f) \le \mathrm{R}(f) \text{ and } \widetilde{\deg}(f)\le 2\mathrm{Q}(f),\ \text{ for total AND partial } f\)
    BdW02 BBCMdW01
    The polynomial method is setting-agnostic: the acceptance probability of any algorithm is a polynomial of degree $\le$ (twice) the number of queries, whatever the domain. Theorem 15 of [BdW02] for the randomized case -- average the leaf-indicator polynomials of the deterministic trees in the mixture, with no constant loss at all -- and Theorem 18 for the quantum one. The approximation constraints are imposed only at the points of $\mathrm{Dom}(f)$, which is why this is the record for the whole family; the total case is inherited from here, and it is tight there ($\mathrm{PARITY}$).

Measures that survive the move to partial functions unchanged: $\deg$-based lower bounds, $\mathrm{Adv}^{\pm}$ (still $=\Theta(\mathrm{Q})$), $\mathrm{prt}$, and the trivial orderings $\mathrm{Q}\le\mathrm{R}\le\mathrm{R}_0\le\mathrm{D}$.

Measures that become meaningless or trivial: $\mathrm{s}$, $\mathrm{bs}$, $\mathrm{C}$ and friends can all be $O(1)$ while $\mathrm{D}=n$, because a promise can force the "certificate" to be the promise itself.

see also: \(\widetilde{\deg}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{R}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{Q}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{Adv}^{\pm}(f)\), Total functions, partial functions, and relations data/relations/06-settings.yaml

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\widetilde{\deg}(\mathrm{PARITY}_n) = n = 2\,\mathrm{Q}(\mathrm{PARITY}_n)\)
    witness: \(\oplus_n\)

The easy direction $\widetilde{\deg}\le 2\mathrm{Q}$ is the polynomial method, so it is recorded for partial $f$ and inherited here; $\mathrm{PARITY}$ shows it is tight already for total $f$.

Open problem 4 of [BdW02]: is $\mathrm{Q}(f)=O(\widetilde{\deg}(f))$ for total $f$? Known false for partial functions -- exponentially so [AmbainisBelovs23] -- and false even for total search problems [BenDavidKundu24search]. For total Boolean functions the best known is $\mathrm{Q} = O(\widetilde{\deg}^4)$, with a quartic separation from cheat sheets [ABK16], so this cell is settled at exponent 4.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\deg(\mathrm{SEARCH}^{\le 1}_n) = 1 \text{ while } \widetilde{\deg}(\mathrm{SEARCH}^{\le 1}_n) = \Theta(\sqrt n)\)
    witness: \(\mathrm{SEARCH}^{\le 1}_n\) BBCMdW01

The usual one-line argument -- "a representing polynomial is in particular an approximating one" -- breaks on a promise, and the failure is not cosmetic. For partial $f$, \(\deg(f)\) asks only that $p$ agree with $f$ on $\mathrm{Dom}(f)$ and lets $p$ be arbitrary elsewhere, whereas \(\widetilde{\deg}_{\varepsilon}(f)\) additionally demands $|p(x)| \le 1+\varepsilon$ at every $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ -- the condition that makes $\widetilde{\deg}$ a quantum lower bound in the first place. On \(\mathrm{SEARCH}^{\le 1}_n\) ($|x| \le 1$; is $|x| = 1$?) the polynomial $\sum_i x_i$ represents $f$ exactly on the domain, so $\deg = 1$, but it runs up to $n$ off the promise; a bounded approximation needs degree $\Theta(\sqrt n)$, matching $\mathrm{Q}$.

see also: \(\widetilde{\deg}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\deg(f)\), \(\mathrm{rdeg}(f)\), \(\mathrm{SEARCH}^{\le 1}_n\) data/relations/09-chain.yaml

Upper bounds — holds for every total

  • \(\widetilde{\deg}(f\circ g) = O\big(\widetilde{\deg}(f)\,\widetilde{\deg}(g)\big)\)
    Sherstov12robust
    Robustification: every bounded polynomial of degree $d$ has a degree-$O(d)$ version that is robust to noisy inputs, so the outer approximating polynomial can be fed noisy copies of the inner ones for free.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\widetilde{\deg}(f\circ g) = \tilde\Omega\big(\sqrt{\mathrm{bs}(f)}\cdot\widetilde{\deg}(g)\big)\)
    CKMPSS23
    The first inner composition theorem for approximate degree with a nontrivial outer measure. It gives composition whenever $\widetilde{\deg}(f) = \Theta(\sqrt{\mathrm{bs}(f)})$.

Open in general, in both the total and partial settings. Known for symmetric outer $f$, and for the special pairs used in the AC$^0$ approximate-degree literature (via dual block composition).

see also: \(\widetilde{\deg}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\deg(f)\), \(\mathrm{bs}(f)\), comp-R, Does approximate degree compose? data/relations/04-composition.yaml

\(\widetilde{\deg}_{\varepsilon}(f) \text{ as } \varepsilon \to 0 \text{ and } \varepsilon\to 1/2\) total Settled parameter: eps #

Upper bounds — holds for every total

  • \(\widetilde{\deg}_\varepsilon(f) = \Theta\big(\widetilde{\deg}_{1/3}(f) + \sqrt{n\log(1/\varepsilon)}\big)\quad (f \text{ symmetric})\)
    deWolf08eps Sherstov08incl
    An exact characterisation for symmetric $f$ -- so, unlike the generic $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ amplification recorded one setting up, a genuinely total-function statement. [Sherstov08incl] proved it up to logs; [deWolf08eps] removed them using the quantum-algorithm view.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\lim_{\gamma\to 0}\widetilde{\deg}_{1/2-\gamma}(f) = \mathrm{sdeg}(f)\)
    As the error approaches $1/2$ the approximate degree degenerates to sign degree -- the $\mathsf{PP}$ / unbounded-error regime. So the whole $\varepsilon$-family interpolates between $\deg$ ($\varepsilon=0$) and $\mathrm{sdeg}$ ($\varepsilon\to1/2$).

The $\varepsilon\to 1/2$ end is where $\mathrm{sdeg}$, $\mathrm{PostQ}$ and $\mathrm{rdeg}_\varepsilon$ live; the $\varepsilon\to 0$ end is where $\deg$ and $\mathrm{Q}_E$ live. The zoo's default $\varepsilon = 1/3$ sits in the middle purely by convention.

see also: \(\widetilde{\deg}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\deg(f)\), \(\mathrm{sdeg}(f)\), \(\mathrm{rdeg}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{PostQ}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{Q}_{\varepsilon}(f)\) data/relations/07-parameters.yaml

Upper bounds — holds for every partial

  • \(\widetilde{\deg}_\varepsilon(f) = O\big(\widetilde{\deg}_{1/3}(f)\log(1/\varepsilon)\big) \text{ in general}\)
    Amplify with a low-degree amplification polynomial: if $A$ has degree $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$, maps $[0,1]$ into $[0,1]$, $[0,1/3]$ into $[0,\varepsilon]$ and $[2/3,1]$ into $[1-\varepsilon,1]$, then $A \circ p$ works. Nothing here looks at the domain: the partial-setting definition of $\widetilde{\deg}$ already demands $p \in [0,1]$ off the promise, which is exactly the hypothesis $A$ needs, so the amplification is setting-agnostic.
see also: \(\widetilde{\deg}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\deg(f)\), \(\mathrm{sdeg}(f)\), \(\mathrm{Q}_{\varepsilon}(f)\) data/relations/07-parameters.yaml

params.name: eps
params.dependence:
• Error reduction: $\widetilde{\deg}_{\varepsilon}(f)=O(\widetilde{\deg}_{1/3}(f)\log(1/\varepsilon))$ (compose with an amplifying univariate polynomial).
  • $\varepsilon\to 0$: $\widetilde{\deg}_0(f)=\deg(f)$, and $\deg(f)=O(\widetilde{\deg}(f)^2)$, so the whole range $\varepsilon\in(0,1/3]$ spans at most a quadratic factor for total $f$.
  • Large error / small bias: $\widetilde{\deg}_{1/2-\gamma}(f)$ can be far smaller; at $\gamma\to 0$ it degenerates towards sign degree \(\mathrm{sdeg}(f)\). The "large-error approximate degree" $\widetilde{\deg}_{1/2-1/\mathrm{poly}}$ is its own subject with applications to $\mathsf{PP}$ and to communication complexity.

facts: $\widetilde{\deg}(f) \le 2\,\mathrm{Q}(f)$: the polynomial method [BBCMdW01].

$\mathrm{D}(f) = O(\widetilde{\deg}(f)^4)$ [ABKRT21], improving $O(\widetilde{\deg}^6)$ [BBCMdW01]; matching separation $\mathrm{D}=\tilde\Omega(\widetilde{\deg}^4)$ [ABBLSS17]. Exponent settled at 4.

Read-once formulas: $\widetilde{\deg}(f)=\Theta(\sqrt n)$ [ABKRT21, Thm 6].

No bound is recorded here directly; the cell is filled by closure through $\widetilde{\deg}\le\deg = \widetilde O(\mathrm{rdeg}^3)$ [KKWY26]. This is the cell with the best known separation from $\mathrm{rdeg}$, so it is also the one where the surviving exponent gap is narrowest from below. Known in the other direction: $\mathrm{rdeg}(f)\le\widetilde{\deg}(f)$ and $\mathrm{rdeg}(f)\le\deg(f)$; also $\mathrm{rdeg}(f) = \Theta(\widetilde{\deg}(f))$ for symmetric $f$.

up.note: Stated natively for query complexity in [JainKlauck10, Thm 3.6], and the proof is a one-liner worth knowing: throw away every subcube with $2^{|A|} > \mathrm{prt}^{\mathrm{LP}}/\varepsilon$ (they carry total weight $\le \varepsilon$), and let $p(x) = \sum_{A \ni x} w_{A,1}$ be the sum of the surviving $1$-labelled monomials. The completeness constraint gives $p \le 1$ everywhere, correctness gives $p \ge 1-2\varepsilon$ on $f^{-1}(1)$ and $p \le 2\varepsilon$ on $f^{-1}(0)$, and $\deg p \le \log(\mathrm{prt}^{\mathrm{LP}}/\varepsilon)$.
